taxonomy.subtopic: Venous outflow collapse and loss of the arteriovenous perfusion gradient

questions.stem_html: A 27-year-old man with a closed tibial fracture develops rapidly worsening leg pain despite opioid therapy. The pain increases with passive toe extension, and the anterior compartment is tense. Diastolic blood pressure is 62 mm Hg, and compartment pressure is 40 mm Hg. The accompanying pressure diagram shows progressive narrowing of the perfusion gradient. Which event most directly initiates the self-amplifying ischemic cycle?

options.text_html: Systemic activation of disseminated intravascular coagulation
Immediate occlusion of the proximal tibial artery by the intact fascia
Compression of low-pressure venules with impaired outflow and rising capillary hydrostatic pressure
Primary failure of lymphatic smooth muscle contraction
Reflex sympathetic constriction of all collateral arteries in the limb

questions.explanation_html: In a closed, noncompliant fascial compartment, bleeding and edema raise interstitial pressure. Low-pressure venules are compressed before higher-pressure arteries, reducing venous outflow and the arteriovenous pressure gradient. Capillary filtration increases, which worsens edema, further elevates compartment pressure and eventually compromises arterial inflow. The delta pressure here is 22 mm Hg, supporting dangerous loss of perfusion.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Large-artery occlusion is not required for compartment syndrome; early ischemia results from microvascular perfusion failure within a pressurized compartment.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Sympathetic vasoconstriction is not the primary initiating mechanism and would not explain the local positive-feedback cycle after fracture swelling.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Lymphatic dysfunction may impair fluid clearance but does not constitute the central early hemodynamic event.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a systemic consumptive coagulopathy and is not the usual cause of localized post-fracture compartment pressure elevation.

questions.educational_objective: Rising pressure in a closed compartment first impairs venous outflow, lowers the arteriovenous perfusion gradient and increases edema, creating a positive-feedback cycle of microvascular ischemia.
